newsitem.title: FRANCE: Luxury king Bernard Arnault pulls off DFS megadeal.
newsitem.headline: Luxury king Bernard Arnault pulls off DFS megadeal.

text.p: Bernard Arnault, the chairman of the world's largest luxury group LVMH and one of the richest men in France, has extended his empire across the globe with the $2.47 billion purchase of U.S. duty free chain DFS.
LVMH said it closed the deal on Saturday and took control of the firm, which owns 180 shops along the lucrative Pacific Rim, despite a legal challenge from two minority shareholders.
The purchase is LVMH's biggest acquisition and the latest coup by Arnault, 48, who broke into the tightly-knit luxury goods industry in 1984 with an investment of 90 million francs ($16.82 million).

Today he is worth more than 20 billion francs, according to the newspaper Les Echos. He owns the rival daily newspaper La Tribune and the magazine Investir and heads the fourth-largest quoted French company with sales of 30 billion francs.
"It's a matter of finding the right opportunities at the right time," Arnault told Les Echos recently.

LVMH's portfolio includes some of the oldest and finest names in the spirits, perfume and fashion industries -- Christian Dior, Givenchy, Moet & Chandon, Guerlain, Kenzo, Veuve Cliquot, Ruinart, Pommery, Hennessy and Louis Vuitton.

Industry experts say Arnault's success lies in the modern business management he has brought to the group without disturbing the separate cultures that nurture the creative talents at each of the houses.

"First and foremost, he's an outstanding financier," said Cedric Magnelia, an analyst at brokerage CS First Boston. "His role has been to oversee the overarching strategy and allocate money to the businesses with the best growth potential."
Arnault's ascent coincided with a wave of mergers that swept France after the liberalisation of takeover rules in 1986, and he came to symbolise a new breed of tough U.S.-style managers.

The tall and slender businessman who now hobnobs with royalty started off as an outsider. The son of a property developer, he was born in the northern French town of Roubaix in 1949 and retains the reserved manner of the region.

Although his first love was music, he studied mathematics at the most prestigious French university, the Ecole Polytechnique. He worked at the family firm until the election of Socialist president Francois Mitterrand in 1981 prompted him to emigrate.

After spending three years developing properties in Florida without much success, Arnault returned to France when a friend suggested that he put together a bid for a money-losing state conglomerate that the government was eager to sell.

The group, Agache-Willot, owned the Boussac textile firm and the fashion house Christian Dior, which became the cornerstone of Arnault's empire. He sold off Agache-Willot's textile and other assets, sparking a public outcry that he had betrayed the government's trust by stripping the company.
Similar accusations of ruthlessness followed his moves to hire Christian Lacroix away from Jean Patou and his purchase of the designer leather goods firm Celine from its founders.
Arnault's big opportunity arose when the merger of the Moet Hennessy group with Louis Vuitton to form LVMH began to sour.

Louis Vuitton's disgruntled boss Henry Racamier invited Arnault and his partner, British drinks group Guinness Plc, to take stakes in LVMH to check what Racamier perceived as the ambitions of Moet Hennessy chairman Alain Chevalier.
The uneasy four-way partnership turned into a boardroom brawl fit to rival the U.S. television soap opera "Dallas".
Chevalier quit after a failed bid to break up the group, and Racamier was forced out in April 1990 after a court fight. Arnault has since boosted profits by 20 percent.

He has brought marketing experts to an industry whose bosses relied on intuition while protecting the mystique of the brands and encouraging innovation. In a move that shocked the fashion trade last year, he chose eclectic British designer John Galliano to head the most Parisian of the couture houses, Dior.
LVMH has bought leather goods firm Loewe, Fred jewellers, and most recently, the acclaimed Chateau d'Yquem vineyard from a feuding aristocratic family. It shows no signs of slowing down.
The purchase of DFS marks a new phase by allowing LVMH to extend control over the distribution of its products and skim off the fat profits generated at the retail level.
LVMH said the acquisition would boost sales by around 50 percent and operating profit by nearly a third.
Arnault, who once dreamed of being a concert pianist, is married to one, Canadian-born Helene Mercier, and has three children, including two from his first marriage.
($1=5.350 French Franc)
